title: Across the Hall
text:
<entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> sits two blocks past the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> checkpoint — the booth that bleeds amber across the wet street all night, scanning plate and intent and waving you through if you're nobody worth stopping. Tonight <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> is gloriously nobody. He leaves the slug-rail hum of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the gray zone</entity> at the door and trades it for the warmer ruin of home.

He makes it up the stairs on the banister and a bad idea, leaving a dark smear on the wall he'll feel guilty about tomorrow. The second floor announces <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> the way it always does — bass through her door, loud enough that it should bother the building more than it does, and the clatter of something being tested and found wanting. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stands in the hall with his hand flat against his side, blood dark between his fingers, and thinks the thing he always thinks when he arrives here in pieces: the mediclone station on Meridian runs all night and leaves no record that touches her.

He knocks. It comes out softer than a knock should.

The music cuts. The door opens on the chain, then all the way, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> takes him in the way she takes in everything — fast, flat, already sorting what to fix first. Pink hair half out of its updo. Grey-blue eyes measuring the spread of the stain.

"That had better not be yours," she says.

"It's mostly someone else's."

Her eyes stop measuring the stain and start measuring him. "Mostly," she repeats, and doesn't move to widen the door. "Meridian's dark. Third power cut this week, and half the block's crew is out there in the amber with nothing to do but wait for it to come back. You walk in here bleeding, and by morning somebody's traded a story about the guy who bled all over the Pivot's second floor. You know how thin the wall between me and the checkpoint is right now?" She glances past him, down the stairwell, at the smear he left drying on the plaster. "You already painted the evidence on my building."

"I didn't have anywhere else." He shifts his weight and his left hand doesn't quite track where he tells it to go. "Every scanner between here and Meridian's live tonight, even with the grid down. Auxiliary power. The one at <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> came down slow, almost polite. *Asset under file review.* <entity repo="entertainment" guid="81b4e6d0-c2f9-a37e-5d1b-8c4f0a7e3d92">Handed</entity> me a case number like a receipt." He tries a breath and it costs him. "It wasn't about the plate. It was never about the plate."

She reads that too, the way she reads everything, filing it against a total. "You could've talked it out."

"Ninety seconds of the wrong kind of loud. I signed the case number and let them take it. Walked here." He almost laughs and thinks better of it. "Client posted the job complete before I made the second block. Φ1.5 in the account, itemized — one for the work, half for *morale*. And a standing contract, scope to be determined. Strangest money in the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>, and no way to spend it standing up."

"That's the part that scares me." A muscle works in her jaw. For a moment he thinks she's going to hand him a rag and a name two blocks over and shut the door — thinks she's doing the math on him the way she does the math on everything, and coming up with a number she doesn't like.

Then she steps back.

"Inside."

She clears the kitchen table with her forearm — a soldering iron, a half-flayed prosthetic hand, a mug — and none of it lands gently. The tools go to the floor and stay there. She doesn't look at them. She looks at him, and at the brace, and at the boot dragging, and her face is the one she keeps for things that are still fixable if she's fast.

"Shirt," she says.

He gets it half over his head before the wound complains, and she's there, peeling the rest off him like a bandage off skin, brisk, no ceremony. Then she stops being brisk.

She has seen <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hurt before. She has not seen this — all of it at once, under the kitchen light, everything his clothes have been keeping off the record. The long pale seam under his ribs, white with age, clean as a weld. A burn climbing his left shoulder, old and rough and uneven, the kind that took time to become what it is. Marks she can date by color and texture the way she dates components. She reads them, one and then the next, her thumb coming to rest against the burn on his shoulder.

"Stop cataloguing me," he says.

"Stop collecting them," she says, and something moves through her face on the word collecting before she reaches for the kit.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> works the way she works anything that's still fixable — talking to keep him present, hands too busy to shake. Antiseptic first, the industrial copper smell of it filling the space between them. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hisses; she doesn't apologize. She flushes the gash in his side, and her thumb braces flat against the muscle below it to hold the edges while she threads the suture, and he feels the small precise tugs as she closes him, one and then the next, her breath warm and uneven against his collarbone.

Halfway through she turns him — checking how the wound tracks, where it might exit — and her fingers move over him the way a mechanic feels for a seized bolt, reading his skin like braille. They find something that shouldn't be there. A screw head. A machine screw, no more than an inch, threaded at one end, the kind you'd pull out of a servo housing. Worked into the skin just under the shoulder blade. From the floor, when the table went.

Her breathing catches, barely audible. She reaches for the tweezers and works it out without a word — a moment where it doesn't want to come, where she has to coax it, gentle and firm, the way you work something that's embedded itself and decided to stay. Then it slides free with a small sound like a tooth breaking. She sets it on the edge of the kit and doesn't look at it again, and he watches her not react to it, and understands that the not-reacting is costing her.

She goes back in with the tweezers, twice, feeling for what else might be in there. Finds nothing. It was in deep enough it should have gone septic days ago, should have put him down. It hadn't. He'd kept moving, and hadn't known, or hadn't cared to know — and either way she can read the arithmetic of it in the set of her jaw. She takes up the needle again.

Somewhere in the middle of it her eyes go bright and too full, and one of them spills, and the tear runs down. He doesn't tell her she's crying. She'd hate that. He holds still and lets her finish, lets the salt find the raw of him, his hands loose at his sides and not moving. He has been sutured before — by people who were paid, and people who owed him, in mediclone booths shaped like the idea of a person. None of them had ever braced a thumb against him like he was worth keeping still.

"You keep doing this," she says, not a question, tying off the last stitch and cutting the thread. Her hands don't shake, but they stop, resting flat on the table either side of him. "Coming back in pieces. Making me put you back together."

"You're good at it."

"That's not the part I'm complaining about."

She should be done. The wound is closed, the forearm is wrapped, the shoulder is taped. Her job — the named, reasonable part of it — is over. And she doesn't move away.

Her hand is still flat on his stomach where she braced to stitch him. It stays. Then it stops staying still — it moves, slow, down the ridges and over the old burn and along the pale seam under his ribs, reading him the way her eyes read everything, except her eyes are closed now. She traces a scar end to end like she's deciding whether to forgive it.

This is the part where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulls away. He has always pulled away. The reasons are many and not wrong.

He doesn't pull away.

He puts his hand over hers and presses it flatter against him, and lets her feel that his heart is doing something undignified, and when she looks up — startled, all her measuring gone at once — he is already looking back.

She kisses him first, like she's been holding it under her tongue for a year, and he answers with both hands in the pink wreck of her hair. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> climbs into his lap right there on the kitchen chair, careful of the bad side and reckless with all the rest, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulls her sweater off over her head and doesn't track where it lands.

In the lower left of his overlay, his neuretics tick up to amber — the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> checkpoint running its three-block sweep, matching faces. Thirty seconds to auto-clear if he's clean. Longer if the chain has him flagged. The scan pattern shifts across the kitchen window, catching her hair and throwing it red and gold, and every proximity warning his neuretics know how to draw is stacking in his periphery, flagging her weight against him as a tactical liability. He watches the timer. He does not move — chooses not to, with full clarity, the way he has never once chosen. For eleven years he stayed a step ahead of every cost. Tonight he lets this one find him. The overlay times out and goes dark.

The last of the tools go off the table — screws skittering across the concrete and into the dark under the workbench, the soldering iron rolling to the edge and catching — and neither of them flinches. Her hands go everywhere they spent the last hour finding wounds, and aren't looking for anything now. His mouth finds the freckled line of her throat and she makes a sound — low, helpless, nothing like her usual register — that she would deny making.

"Bed," she manages, "is eight feet —"

"Too far?" he asks, against her skin.

She laughs, breathless, like something held too long has finally let go, and closes the eight feet.

He stands with her wrapped around him. His side screams; he tells it to wait. They make it as far as the wall, which is close and enough. Her hand fists in his hair and pulls him back to her mouth. Her fingers drag down his back and find new scars to learn. His hands close over her — the compact, strong shape of her — and pull her tighter. His palms move slow across her ribs, her spine, the warm dip at the small of her back.

She gasps his name into the crook of his neck, like it's something she's allowed now. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>." His breath goes ragged. He does nothing to hide it. His shoulders drop. For eleven years he has kept himself at the exact distance where nothing can reach him — you don't survive by feeling, you survive by moving, by staying ahead, by never letting anything get close enough to cost you. Tonight he lets the wall take their weight and stops keeping it.

Then her palm flattens over his heart and she stills. Draws back an inch, her forehead against his. Her eyes search his in the low light, and he knows what she's asking without the words — the same question that has always stood between them: whether he'll be gone by morning, whether this is the thing she gets to keep or only borrow. She doesn't say it. But her hand stays flat against his chest, splayed, reading the rhythm underneath, holding him at that last inch of distance, waiting for something he isn't sure he can promise. His side chooses that moment to knife through him, sharp enough that he flinches, and for a breath the old instinct rises — pull back, put the wall between them, keep himself where nothing can reach. Fear and pain are the same frequency; eleven years of contracts taught him that. He feels her feel it. Her fingers tighten, ready to let go if he does.

He doesn't. He covers her hand with his own and presses it flatter, harder, past the last inch, lets her feel the whole of it — the speed, the irregularity, the way his body is betraying every rule he ever kept. Her eyes snap to his and he is already looking back, and there is no measuring in her face now, no calculation, just the naked fact of her seeing him. He lets her have the answer even though it terrifies him.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>," he says, and doesn't move his hand away.

They move together — her back against the wall, then the floor. The brick scrapes his spine; her knees hit the concrete first, then his. His mouth at her collarbone. Her hands trace him the way they once closed him up, except now they aren't closing anything. The only sounds are breath and the low thrum of the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> coming up through the concrete. His hand finds hers on the floor and holds it. She curls her fingers through his and holds back.

After, the floor is hard and they don't care.

She lies half on his good side. The apartment ticks and cools around them. Bass from someone else's unit thumps faint through the brick. Down where the wall meets the floor, a thin green light runs the baseboard seam and goes still — lumen mice settling back into the dark — and neither of them looks. His chest goes up and down too fast, then slower. Her pink hair is stuck to her cheek. She doesn't fix it.

She wants one thing now, and she'll get it before the night tips her back into thinking: to learn him by hand until she has all of him memorized, every seam and old break of him, so that whatever tomorrow costs her she'll have this to keep.

She runs a finger along the length of him — the same slow touch she'd use to find what was broken, except now it asks nothing. It's learning a body it means to come back to. The burn on his shoulder. The fresh line of her own stitches, neat as a hem. The dip of his sternum.

He does the same to her. The freckles across her collarbone. The small old scar through one eyebrow. The blunt, strong forearms that put him back together an hour ago. His thumb finds the pulse at the base of her throat and stays there — not counting it, just feeling it move. She lets him. She watches him do it, grey-blue eyes gone soft, and says nothing.

title: The Wall
text:
She moves first. She sits up and reaches for his side — but the hand that reaches now isn't the hand that stitched him an hour ago. This one checks the knot, presses the tape flat, tests the swelling at his shoulder blade where the screw had been. Already yellowing at the edges, faster than it had any right to — his body kept its own calendar these days. Clinical. The touch of someone reading a chart.

He wants her to stay on the near side of that inch — to keep the hand that stitched him, not the one that files him away. He wants to say it. He feels the inch open up between them and doesn't reach across it. The line of her stitches ridges his ribs — a question she asked and then closed. Her thumb crosses the seam once more, lighter, the way a medic checks a response and moves on.

He doesn't make it easier. He doesn't make it harder. He lies still under her hands and lets her pull away.

"This can't happen again," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says. He's looking at the ceiling when he says it.

The words land in the silence she's just built. In the inches between them. In the moment where the wall is still settling, still deciding whether it will hold.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> props herself up on one elbow, forearm flat on the concrete, and looks at him. She has the calm of someone who has already won an argument the other person doesn't know is over. She doesn't answer. She reaches for the screw on the floor beside them — the machine screw, the one she pulled from his shoulder blade an hour ago, still wearing a thin smear of blood — and picks it up between two fingers. She turns it once in the low light, reading it the way she reads everything broken. Then she sets it on the concrete beside her knee, precise as filing evidence.

His thumb is still at the base of her throat, where he left it. He doesn't move it.

She doesn't answer right away.

That's the answer.

She turns onto her side, facing the room instead of him, and takes the words in. She doesn't argue with them. She doesn't let them go either.

"Okay," she says.

One word. It lands where it lands — not to him, to the act of it, like a tool set down.

She stands. She finds her shirt on the floor near the kitchen chair and pulls it over her head in one motion, back turned, easy in her own body, with no performance left to give. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watches the line of her spine — the small scar behind her left shoulder from a thermal calibration slip he'd watched her bandage herself two months ago. She doesn't look back.

She pulls on the rest of what's hers, works the zipper free where it catches without cursing at it, the same hands that were inside his forearm an hour ago closing off the night with the same economy. She picks the soldering iron up off the floor and stands the mug upright — not tidying, just marking the night finished. The iron's still warm. She thumbs the base to check the element's cool enough to coil the cord, and coils it, and sets it where it belongs. Habit. In the grey zone you don't leave a live tip on a floor; a stray amp finds its way home eventually, and homes here are dry wood and older wiring.

"You should sleep," she says. She says it toward the counter, not at him. Her professional voice. The one that means the visit is over and the patient is stable.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>."

She looks over her shoulder.

He has nothing to follow it with. The name is the whole of it. He said it to stop her being so cleanly competent, and it worked, and now they're both in it — the kitchen at 2E, the tools on the floor, the twelve inches of air between them that is both enormous and nowhere near enough.

Her hand moves like it might say something — touch his shoulder, close the distance — then stops. She closes it into a fist and lets it drop. Her expression doesn't change. Something behind it does. She looks at him the way she looks at a system that's asking her a question she already knows the answer to.

"Sleep," she says again, and this time it sounds like she means it for both of them.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> crosses the hall at 02:47 with his ribs taped, his shoulder stiff, and a cut from wrist to elbow, bled through field strip. It always scars when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> stitches him. She doesn't pull the thread any tighter than she has to — and that isn't the reason it scars.

2D in the dark. His door. His space.

He hangs his jacket on the hook, sits on the edge of the bed, and looks at nothing for a while before he lies down. There's nothing to be done tonight. The body needs sleep, and the body is still his to send there.

The wall between 2D and 2E is ferrocement — fourteen centimeters, load-bearing. <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> was built before the corps figured out how to make everything disposable, and it carries sound the way old buildings do, honest and unhurried. Tonight it carries nothing across. She's being quiet. He's being quiet. The building does the breathing for both of them.

The lumen mice trace the ceiling. The Atlas array runs its rest-hour check — unhurried, nominal — and reports nothing he asked about. Twelve inches of air on the other side of the wall. The same twelve inches there have always been. Except a door oiled on one side only makes a different sound now, and he knows the sound, and his ear finds it before he can tell it not to.

He closes his eyes. He's good at not thinking about things. Better at it than almost anyone he knows.

Tomorrow he'll oil his own door. He'll get the can from the maintenance shelf in the basement, the one that smells like machine shops and the before-times, and he'll do both sides, loud enough that she hears him do it. Loud enough that she has to know he's doing it on purpose. Let her wonder what he knows. That's the move: stop pretending the twelve inches are what they were, and make her be the one who flinches first. Put the boundary back where it belongs and make a ceremony of it, so it holds.

The ceiling is dark. The mice do their slow work.

He doesn't think about it at all.
